chunks: "ACR is the effective resistance of an inductor's winding at the operating frequency.
It's higher than the DC resistance because at AC the current doesn't spread evenly through the wire. There are two reasons.

The first is skin effect: the changing magnetic field inside the conductor induces eddy currents that oppose the current in the center and reinforce it near the surface, so the current crowds into a skin whose depth is delta equals root of rho over pi f mu.
For copper that's 66 micrometers at 1 megahertz and 0. 2 millimeters at 100 kilohertz.
When the wire is thicker than a couple of skin depths, only the outer layer carries current, so the resistance goes up as the square root of frequency.
The second is the proximity effect: in a winding, each turn sits in the magnetic field of its neighbors, which induces eddy currents that further crowd the current.
In multi-layer windings, this is usually worse than skin effect alone, and it rises quickly with the number of layers.
Practically, a 1 millimeter wire at 500 kilohertz has an AC resistance about three times its DC resistance from skin effect alone, and in a multi-layer coil, many times more.
So, to reduce it, you use Litz wire, which has many thin insulated strands, or foil, fewer layers, and interleaving.
Core loss also shows up as an effective series resistance in measurements, so measured ACR of a cored inductor includes it."
